summary: Clean-code policy for keeping everyday product code readable, small, testable, and safe for coding agents to modify.
description: A portable clean-code pack for projects that want readable files, clear names, small responsibilities, low duplication, useful tests, and simple code that agents can safely change.
plainLanguageSummary: Use this when a project needs code that is easy for humans and agents to read, change, and verify.
bestFor: Product apps where files or helpers are becoming hard to understand
Brownfield projects where agents keep adding duplicate helpers or second patterns
Teams that want simple standards for naming, file size, comments, tests, and responsibility boundaries
notFor: One-off scripts where speed matters more than maintainability
Performance-critical internals that need a separate low-level engineering policy
userQuestions: Which files are too large or doing too many jobs?
Which helpers or names make the code harder to understand?
Which changed behavior needs a focused test before we call it done?
qualityBar: Rules are practical and do not force style-only rewrites.
Agents can apply the pack during normal edits without stopping progress.
The pack protects readability, naming, responsibility, duplication, and test proof.
agentUse: Use this pack after understanding the local code style and existing helpers.
Prefer improving touched code over broad cleanup unrelated to the task.
Escalate to normal lane when a cleanup changes public behavior, shared helpers, or many files.

structureTree.title: Clean-code responsibility tree
structureTree.summary: A practical view of where maintainability concerns usually live. These are code roles, not required folder names.

nodes.label: Behavior owner
nodes.responsibility: Owns product behavior, workflow logic, local validation, and tests for a specific user or system action.
antiPatterns: One file handles input parsing, business rules, persistence, UI mapping, and notifications.

nodes.label: Shared utility owner
nodes.responsibility: Owns stable cross-feature helpers only after reuse is real and the helper has one clear job.
antiPatterns: misc.ts, helpers.ts, utils.ts, or common.ts becomes a bucket for unrelated logic.

nodes.label: Proof owner
nodes.responsibility: Owns focused tests or smoke checks that prove changed behavior and protect important edge cases.
antiPatterns: Behavior changes with only snapshot churn or no focused proof.

beforeEditing: Find the local naming, helper, and test patterns before adding new code.
Identify the smallest owner for the behavior being changed.
Check whether a helper already exists before adding a new one.
beforeDone: Confirm touched files still have one clear responsibility.
Confirm any new helper has a specific name and real caller.
Confirm changed behavior has focused proof or an explicit reason proof was skipped.

appliesWhen.summary: The task changes product source code, shared helpers, tests, or behavior-bearing files.
evidence: Source files under src, app, packages, features, modules, or services are being changed
The task adds helpers, validation, components, services, or tests

appliesWhen.summary: The project has large files, duplicated helpers, vague names, weak tests, or mixed responsibilities.
evidence: Helpers named misc, common, or utils
Repeated local parsing or formatting logic

avoidWhen.summary: Generated or vendored files should not be cleaned manually.
evidence: Path contains generated, vendor, dist, build, or node_modules

avoidWhen.summary: Unrelated cleanup should not be mixed into a focused behavior change.
evidence: Cleanup touches files outside the task scope
No bug, feature, or readability reason is tied to the touched code

rules.title: One clear responsibility
rules.summary: A touched file or function should have one clear job. Split or move code when one place handles unrelated behavior, transport, persistence, formatting, and UI concerns together.
rules.rationale: Small ownership makes agent edits safer and human review easier.
examples: Keep input parsing at the boundary and product behavior in the feature/service.
Extract a named helper when a branch has a reusable, clear concept.
antiPatterns: A file handles request parsing, business rules, persistence, email, and response shaping.
A component owns data fetching, formatting, mutation logic, and complex layout state.

rules.title: Names say the purpose
rules.summary: Names should describe the domain idea or technical responsibility. Avoid vague names such as misc, helper, data, thing, manager, or utils when a specific name is possible.
rules.rationale: Clear names reduce repeated explanation and help agents find the right code.
antiPatterns: data variable hides whether the value is user input, database output, or API output

rules.title: Shared code is proven
rules.summary: Do not move code into shared helpers until at least two real callers need the same stable behavior.
rules.rationale: Speculative shared code becomes a dumping ground and makes future changes harder.
examples: Keep feature-only logic inside the feature.
Move formatting code to shared only after multiple features use the same behavior.
antiPatterns: Create shared/helpers.ts before reuse is proven.
Move one feature's private business rule into shared.

rules.title: Boundaries parse unknowns
rules.summary: Parse and normalize unknown external data at boundaries. Do not spread defensive unknown checks through core product logic.
rules.rationale: Core code stays simpler when uncertainty is handled at the edge.
examples: Validate request body before calling the use case.
Normalize webhook payload in the adapter.
antiPatterns: Every service function checks whether the same field is a string.
UI components repeatedly defend against impossible server shapes.

rules.title: Comments explain why
rules.summary: Use comments for non-obvious decisions, constraints, or tradeoffs. Do not add comments that repeat what the code already says.
rules.rationale: Useful comments preserve context; noisy comments make files harder to scan.
examples: Explain why a retry limit is lower than normal.
Link a temporary workaround to an owner or issue.
antiPatterns: TODO has no owner, reason, or removal condition.

rules.title: Changed behavior has proof
rules.summary: When behavior changes, add or run focused proof that would fail if the behavior were wrong.
rules.rationale: Clean code is not only readable; it must be safe to change.
examples: Run the feature test that covers the changed branch.
Add a focused unit test for a new parsing rule.
antiPatterns: Only run formatting after changing behavior.
Close work with no test, smoke check, or skipped-proof reason.
